q: 1. The weight of vehicles affects
explain: Pavement thickness is structurally designed based on the magnitude of wheel loads and axle weights to prevent fatigue and rutting.

q: 2. On most smooth hard surfaced roads, rolling resistance to moving vehicles, ranges from
explain: For standard hard pavements, the rolling resistance typically falls within the 9 to 11 kg per tonne range.

q: 3. The distance travelled by revolving the wheel of a vehicle more than its circumferential movement, is known as
explain: Slip occurs when the wheel rotates more than the actual distance covered (common during acceleration on slippery surfaces).

q: 4. Longitudinal pavement lines marked broken in white paint
options: are for the guidance of the drivers
are not to be crossed over
may be crossed over at the discretion of the driver
explain: Broken white lines indicate that lane changing or overtaking is permitted when safe; solid lines indicate crossing is prohibited.

q: 5. The top of the ground on which the foundation of road rests, is called ............
explain: The sub-grade is the naturally occurring or prepared soil bed that supports the entire pavement structure.

q: 6. The foundation of a road is also called ............
explain: In older terminology, the foundation layer providing structural strength is often referred to as soling or the base course.

q: 7. The super structure of a road is called ............
explain: The uppermost layer in direct contact with traffic is the 'super structure,' commonly called the wearing course or road surfacing.

q: 8. The thickness of base, in no case, should be more than ............
explain: For efficient compaction and structural performance, individual base course layers are typically limited to a maximum thickness of 20 cm.

q: 9. The road surfacing should be ............
explain: To protect the lower layers and handle traffic, the surface must resist water penetration (impervious), withstand wear (durable), and maintain its shape under load (stable).

q: 10. The thickness of road surfacing depends upon the ............
explain: Pavement thickness design considers the load (type/intensity of traffic) and the structural properties of the materials used.

q: 11. The shape of the camber provided for cement concrete pavement is ............
explain: Straight-line cambers are preferred for concrete pavements because they are easier to construct and maintain with rigid slabs.

q: 12. A water bound macadam road is an example of ............
explain: WBM (Water Bound Macadam) consists of crushed stone layers held together by water and stone dust; it behaves as a flexible pavement.

q: 13. A cement grouted road is an example of ............ pavement.
explain: Cement grouted pavements have higher stiffness than flexible ones but less than a full RC slab, classifying them as semi-rigid.

q: 14. The flexible pavement distribute the wheel load ............
options: through a set of layers to sub-grade
explain: Flexible pavements distribute loads through grain-to-grain contact across various layers (surface, base, sub-base) down to the sub-grade.

q: 15. The structure of a road is composed of ............
explain: A standard pavement structure includes the sub-grade (foundation), sub-base, base, and the surface wearing course.

q: 16. The natural soil on which the pavement rests and to which the entire load of structure is ultimately transferred, is known as the ............
explain: The sub-grade is the bottom-most layer consisting of natural or compacted soil that bears the total load of the road.

q: 17. The sub-base course is placed immediately above the ............
explain: The sub-base is the layer directly on top of the sub-grade soil.

q: 18. The wearing course in the case of flexible pavements consist of ............
options: broken stone and granular material mixed with tar
a mixture of bituminous material and aggregate
explain: For modern flexible pavements, the wearing course is typically a mix of aggregate and a bituminous binder (asphalt).

q: 19. The selection of design curve in Wyoming method of flexible pavement design, is based upon ............
explain: The Wyoming method uses a chart-based design that adjusts for climate factors like rainfall, water table depth, and frost.

q: 20. The California bearing ratio (C.B.R.) method of flexible pavement design gives an idea about ............
options: the quality of road making material
explain: CBR is an empirical test that relates soil strength/stiffness to pavement thickness required for specific traffic levels.

q: 21. In C.B.R. test, the value of C.B.R. is calculated at ............
explain: CBR values are determined for both 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm penetration, and the higher value is usually reported.

q: 22. Which of the following method is recommended by I.R.C. for design of flexible pavement?
explain: The Indian Roads Congress (IRC:37) adopts the CBR method for the design of flexible pavements.

q: 23. The group index method of designing flexible pavement is ............
options: an empirical method based on the physical properties of the sub-grades soil
an empirical method based on the strength characteristics of the sub-grade soil
explain: The Group Index (GI) is calculated using soil properties like liquid limit, plasticity index, and the percentage passing the 75-micron sieve.

q: 24. The value of group index of a soil varies from ............
explain: The Group Index formula yields values between 0 (very good sub-grade) and 20 (very poor sub-grade).

q: 25. The minimum thickness of the base of a flexible pavement is kept as ............
explain: A minimum of 10 cm is generally required for the base course to ensure proper load distribution and construction stability.

q: 26. The main advantage of concrete pavements is that ............
options: it offers less resistance to traffic
it is not slippery when clean
explain: Rigid (concrete) pavements are durable, provide a smooth riding surface, and require significantly less maintenance over their long lifespan compared to flexible ones.

q: 27. The depth of reinforcement, below the surface of pavement, is kept as ............
explain: A standard clear cover of 50 mm is typically provided for reinforcement in concrete pavements to protect the steel from corrosion and surface wear.

q: 28. Of all the forces stressing a concrete pavement, the most significant are those imposed by the ............
explain: While temperature causes warping, the primary structural design of concrete pavement is governed by the heavy concentrated wheel loads of vehicles.

q: 29. A large difference of temperature between the top and the bottom of the slab causes ............ of the slab.
explain: Temperature gradients cause the top and bottom of the slab to expand or contract at different rates, leading to 'warping' or curling of the slab edges.

q: 30. When the exposed surface of a pavement dries and shrinks more than the underlying concrete, a phenomenon known as ............ of the surface may occur.
explain: Crazing refers to a network of fine hairline cracks on the surface caused by rapid drying and shrinkage of the top layer of concrete.

q: 31. The joints, parallel to the centre-line of the road, are called ............
explain: Longitudinal joints run in the direction of traffic (parallel to the centerline) to control longitudinal cracking and delineate lanes.

q: 32. The longitudinal joints are provided when the width of road is more than ............
explain: For pavements wider than approximately 4 meters, longitudinal joints are necessary to prevent irregular longitudinal cracks caused by subgrade movement or warping.

q: 33. The longitudinal joints may be ............
explain: Various joint designs are used in concrete construction to ensure load transfer or to provide a controlled plane of weakness for cracking.

q: 34. Longitudinal joints in concrete pavements ............
options: take care of the unequal settlement of the sub-grade
help in laying out concrete in convenient widths
explain: Longitudinal joints serve functional purposes for traffic (lanes), structural safety (settlement), and construction efficiency.

q: 35. The longitudinal joint in concrete pavements, as recommended by I.R.C., is of ............
explain: IRC recommends the use of tied or hinged joints for longitudinal purposes to keep the slabs from separating while allowing for rotation.

q: 36. The transverse joint may be a ............
explain: Transverse joints run perpendicular to the road centerline and include joints designed for expansion, contraction, or warping.

q: 37. To prevent the development of excessive compressive stresses in the concrete pavements as a result of expansion caused by increase in temperature, the type of transverse joint provided is ............
explain: Expansion joints contain a compressible filler material that allows concrete slabs to expand during hot weather without crushing each other.

q: 38. The maximum spacing of contraction joints in unreinforced concrete slabs for a slab thickness of 20 cm is ............
explain: To prevent random cracking due to shrinkage, unreinforced slabs require closely spaced contraction joints, typically 4.5 m apart for standard thicknesses.

q: 39. The dowel bars are used in rigid pavements for ............
options: transferring load from one portion to another
explain: Dowel bars are smooth steel bars placed across transverse joints to transfer wheel loads from one slab to the next, ensuring smooth transitions.

q: 40. Transverse contraction joints relieve ............ stresses in concrete.
explain: Concrete is weak in tension. Contraction joints allow the slab to shorten during cooling or drying, relieving the internal tensile stresses that cause cracking.

q: 41. Weight of a vehicle affects ............
explain: Heavier vehicle loads exert higher stresses on the road, which directly determines the required thickness and strength of the pavement layers.
